strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: forecasting pretraining loss early enough to guide decisions on the target model. Modeling loss by token position offers an interpretable empirical perspective on training dynamics.

The experimental study spans LLaMA-style models from 9.8M to 6.7B parameters, with additional GPT-NeoX and MoE fitting experiments. Evaluation includes in-distribution and out-of-distribution text, plus LAMBADA and WikiText.

The forecasting experiments evaluate subsequent, unseen training checkpoints using prefixes covering 10–40% of training. Figures 3 and 5 report consistent improvements over the three tested baselines, providing evidence beyond retrospective curve fitting.

The data-mixture application connects forecasting to completed training runs: the selected configurations improve perplexity in all four reported settings and downstream performance in 12 of 14 comparisons. Architecture tables, package versions, equations, and pseudocode provide useful implementation guidance.
weaknesses: The decisive forecasting comparison does not isolate the contribution of token-position modeling. The proposed method incorporates a piecewise trajectory and the known cosine schedule, whereas the baselines use simple aggregate-loss functions. After a0 and a1 are frozen, Eq. (10) itself becomes a constant plus a2. A direct aggregate-loss predictor with comparable schedule information and functional flexibility is essential to establish the claimed advantage.

A material inconsistency affects the justification for the hyperbolic form: Section 2.3 reports power-law R² below 0.75 for over 95% of checkpoints, while Table 9 reports R² above 0.95 for 67% of the 58M/ID-Val checkpoints. These accounts require reconciliation before the comparative fitting evidence can be assessed confidently.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The outlier-removal threshold, nonlinear-fitting initialization and constraints, evaluation interval, and actual candidate mixture weights are unspecified; no implementation or recorded loss trajectories are identified. Algorithm 1 also applies calibration when Npred ≤ Nsep, contradicting Section 2.4's requirement for post-separation observations. These details directly affect extrapolation and need clarification.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence is promising but limited. The application forecasts from 10B tokens, only 2.5% of training, whereas the systematic forecasting evaluation starts at 10%. Predicted and final losses across all five candidates, ranking accuracy, and uncertainty are not reported. The modest perplexity gains lack independent-run variability estimates; averaging the last five checkpoints does not provide those estimates. A comparison at matched search cost would also strengthen the efficiency claim.

The scope and novelty claims exceed the demonstrated evidence. Kaplan et al. already analyze training curves, and the manuscript itself cites Luo et al. (2025) on loss-curve prediction across learning-rate schedules. The specific token-position formulation needs clearer positioning. Moreover, the additional architectures and linear schedule are evaluated primarily through retrospective fitting, so their forecasting generalization remains unestablished.

The theoretical interpretations need qualification. Equation (17) follows from manually freezing a0 and a1; equal observed loss decreases do not establish that position-based weighting is unnecessary. The three suppression experiments support a narrower empirical conclusion. Appendix C also rejects exponential decay by setting its additive offset to zero, although the stated exponential family permits a positive asymptote. These arguments do not establish the claimed theoretical preference for the proposed form.
